title: ClickHouse
description: A ClickHouse database — self-hosted or ClickHouse Cloud — over its HTTP interface.

setup.title: Where it is
setup.say:
ClickHouse's HTTP address — https://<host>:8443 for ClickHouse Cloud, http://<host>:8123 for one of your own.

If it lets in only known addresses (ClickHouse Cloud: Settings → IP access list), let the engine's machine in first.

setup.title: A user that may read
setup.say: The database to read and a user that may read it — run this as an admin (choose a password):

copy.label: Make a read-only user
copy.value:
CREATE USER superatom IDENTIFIED BY 'choose-a-password' SETTINGS readonly = 1;
GRANT SELECT ON your_database.* TO superatom;

title: DuckDB
description: DuckDB: a DuckDB file on the engine, files in storage or on the web (Parquet, CSV, JSON — S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure, R2, https), or MotherDuck.

fields.name: source
fields.label: What it reads
fields.help: file: a DuckDB database file on the engine's machine · files: Parquet, CSV or JSON files in storage or on the web · motherduck: a MotherDuck database

fields.name: path
fields.label: Database file
fields.help: Its path on the engine's machine (a relative path is in the engine's data directory).

fields.name: files
fields.label: Its tables
fields.help: One table a line: its name, then where its files are. A * reads every matching file as one table; .parquet, .csv and .json are read as they are.

fields.name: storage
fields.label: How it gets in
fields.help: public: anyone may read them (https, public buckets) · s3: a key for S3 or anything that speaks it (AWS, Cloudflare R2, MinIO, or a Google Cloud Storage HMAC key) · azure: an Azure Storage connection string

fields.name: region
fields.label: Region
fields.help: AWS: the bucket's region. R2: auto.

fields.name: endpoint
fields.label: Endpoint
fields.help: Only for one that is not AWS: Cloudflare R2 (<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com — and write its files as s3://bucket/…), MinIO (its address). Google Cloud Storage needs none: write gs://bucket/…

fields.name: connectionString
fields.label: Connection string
fields.help: Azure portal → the storage account → Access keys → Connection string.

fields.name: token
fields.label: Token
fields.help: MotherDuck → Settings → Access tokens.

setup.title: What it reads
setup.say:
DuckDB reads from many places. Choose where your data is:

1. file — a DuckDB database file on the engine's machine.
2. files — Parquet, CSV or JSON files: in S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure, Cloudflare R2, or at an https address.
3. motherduck — a database in MotherDuck.

setup.title: Where it is
setup.say: Where the data is. For files, one table a line — its name, then where its files are: s3://bucket/path/*.parquet (AWS, R2, MinIO), gs://bucket/… (Google Cloud Storage), az://container/… (Azure), or https://…

setup.title: Letting it in, and reading
setup.say: How it gets in — files anyone may read need nothing; private ones need a key that may read them. Then the engine opens it and reads each table.

fix.say: The storage refused the key: check it may read those files (s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the bucket).
No file is there: check each location — the bucket, the path, and the * pattern.
DuckDB could not load what it needs to read remote files — the engine's machine needs to reach extensions.duckdb.org once.

title: GitHub
description: Repositories, issues and pull requests; open an issue.

fields.name: token
fields.label: Access token
fields.help: A fine-grained personal access token with read access to the repositories (and issues: write, to open issues).

fields.name: owner
fields.label: Owner
fields.help: A user or organisation whose repositories are read first (optional).

setup.title: A token that may read
setup.say: Make a fine-grained token: [GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) — the repositories to read, Contents and Issues: read (Issues: write, to open issues). Give it here.

title: Google Sheets
description: Each person's own spreadsheets in Google Drive: list them, read a sheet's rows — signed in with their own Google account.

setup.title: Your organisation's Google app
setup.say:
People sign in to Google Sheets with their own Google account, through your organisation's own app with Google. An organisation admin sets it once — in [Google Cloud](https://console.cloud.google.com/):

1. APIs & Services → Library: enable the Google Sheets API and the Google Drive API.
2. Google Auth Platform → Get started: name it Superatom, audience External; under Audience add the people who will connect as test users (or publish it).
3. Data access → add the scopes spreadsheets.readonly, drive.metadata.readonly, openid and userinfo.email.
4. Clients → Create client → Web application, with the redirect address below. Copy its client ID and secret.
5. Give them here (Organisation → Connectors → Sign-in apps).

setup.title: Your own Google account
setup.say: Connect your own Google account: the spreadsheets read here are the ones it may see. Google may say it has not verified the app — continue, it is your organisation's own.

fix.say: Google was not allowed: sign in again and tick the Sheets and Drive permissions. If Google says the app is not for you, an admin adds you as a test user (Google Auth Platform → Audience).

title: MCP server
description: Any Model Context Protocol server: its tools become actions, its resources things to read.

fields.name: url
fields.label: Server URL
fields.help: The server's Streamable HTTP endpoint (often ending in /mcp).

fields.name: token
fields.label: Token
fields.help: Sent as a bearer token, if the server needs one.

setup.title: Where the server is
setup.say: The MCP server's address (Streamable HTTP, like https://tools.example.com/mcp).

setup.title: Sign in
setup.say: Its token, if it asks for one.

title: MongoDB
description: A MongoDB database — also MongoDB Atlas and Amazon DocumentDB. Read with find and aggregate, written as JSON.

fields.name: url
fields.label: Connection string
fields.help: With its user and password; kept sealed.

setup.title: Its connection string
setup.say:
The connection string, with a user that may read — mongodb+srv://user:password@cluster.example.net for Atlas (Database → Connect → Drivers), or mongodb://user:password@host:27017.

Atlas lets in only known addresses: Network Access → add the engine's machine first.

fix.say: The cluster's name is not found: copy the connection string again from Atlas (Connect → Drivers).

title: MySQL and MariaDB
description: A MySQL or MariaDB database — also Amazon RDS and Aurora MySQL, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database for MySQL, PlanetScale.

fields.name: ssl
fields.label: SSL
fields.help: require (the default) for anything on a network.

setup.title: Where the database is
setup.say:
The address MySQL answers on, as the engine reaches it — a name like db.example.com, or an IP address. Not "localhost", unless the engine runs on that same machine.

If the database lets in only known addresses (a firewall, an allow-list, a cloud security group), let the engine's machine in first.

setup.title: A user that may read
setup.say: Superatom only reads. Give it a user of its own that may read and nothing more — run this as an admin (choose a password, and name your database):

copy.label: Make a read-only user
copy.value:
CREATE USER 'superatom'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'choose-a-password';
GRANT SELECT, SHOW VIEW ON your_database.* TO 'superatom'@'%';

fix.when: is not allowed to connect|Host '.*' is not allowed
fix.say: MySQL does not let the user in from the engine's address. Make the user for '%' (any address) or for the engine's address.

title: NetSuite
description: Oracle NetSuite through SuiteQL, with an OAuth 2.0 machine-to-machine certificate.

fields.name: privateKey
fields.label: Private key (PEM)
fields.help: The private key of the certificate uploaded to NetSuite.

setup.title: Your NetSuite account
setup.say: Your account ID — in NetSuite, Setup → Company → Company Information → Account ID (like 1234567 or 1234567_SB1 for a sandbox).

setup.title: An integration that may read
setup.say:
NetSuite lets apps in with OAuth 2.0 machine-to-machine:

1. Setup → Integration → Manage Integrations → New: name it Superatom, tick Client Credentials (Machine to Machine), and the scopes REST Web Services and SuiteAnalytics Connect. Save, and copy its Client ID.
2. Make a certificate (the commands below), then Setup → Integration → OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials (M2M) Setup → Create New: the integration, a role that may read, and the certificate's public part. Copy its Certificate ID.
3. Give the private key below.

fix.say: NetSuite refused the integration: check the Client ID and the Certificate ID, that the certificate is mapped to an active role, and that the integration is enabled.

title: Oracle Database
description: An Oracle database — on premises, Oracle Cloud (Autonomous Database), Amazon RDS for Oracle — read through its thin client (no Oracle client installed).

fields.name: schema
fields.label: Schema
fields.help: Whose tables to read; the user's own when empty.

setup.title: Where the database is
setup.say:
The address Oracle answers on, as the engine reaches it — a name like db.example.com, or an IP address. Not "localhost", unless the engine runs on that same machine.

If the database lets in only known addresses (a firewall, an allow-list, a cloud security group), let the engine's machine in first.

setup.title: A user that may read
setup.say: The database's service name (FREEPDB1, ORCLPDB1…) and a user that may read — run this as an admin (choose a password):

copy.label: Make a read-only user

setup.title: Which schema
setup.say: Leave it empty to read the user's own, or name the schema whose tables to read.

title: PostgreSQL
description: A PostgreSQL database — also Amazon RDS and Aurora PostgreSQL, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Supabase, Neon, Redshift's protocol.

fields.name: schemas
fields.label: Schemas
fields.help: Which schemas to read (comma-separated); every schema of the user's when empty.

fields.name: ssl
fields.label: SSL
fields.help: require (the default) for anything on a network.

setup.title: Where the database is
setup.say:
The address PostgreSQL answers on, as the engine reaches it — a name like db.example.com, or an IP address. Not "localhost", unless the engine runs on that same machine.

If the database lets in only known addresses (a firewall, an allow-list, a cloud security group), let the engine's machine in first.

setup.title: A user that may read
setup.say: Superatom only reads. Give it a user of its own that may read and nothing more — run this as an admin of the database (choose a password, and name your database):

copy.label: Make a read-only user

fix.say: The database refuses connections from the engine's address. Add a line for it to pg_hba.conf (host all {user} <the engine's address>/32 scram-sha-256) and reload PostgreSQL.

setup.title: Which schemas
setup.say: Leave it empty to read every schema the user may see, or name the ones to read (public, sales). The check counts the tables it may read there.

fix.say: Signed in, but {user} may read no table there. Give it SELECT on the tables (the commands in the step before), or name a schema it may read.

title: REST API (JSON)
description: Any HTTP API that answers in JSON: name its endpoints, read them as tables.

fields.name: endpoints
fields.label: Endpoints
fields.help: One per line: a name and a path, e.g. “customers /customers”. Each becomes something to read.

fields.name: header
fields.label: Auth header
fields.help: The header the token goes in.

fields.name: token
fields.label: Token
fields.help: Sent as “Bearer <token>” in the auth header, if the API needs one.

setup.title: Where the API is
setup.say: The API's base address (https://api.example.com/v1).

setup.title: What to read, and how to sign in
setup.say: Its endpoints, one per line — a name and a path (customers /customers). Its token, and the header it goes in (Authorization: Bearer, unless the API says otherwise).

title: SA-WAREHOUSE
description: The organisation's warehouse in Superatom: the tables it granted this project, read through the platform.

title: Microsoft SQL Server, Azure SQL, Fabric
description: A SQL Server database, an Azure SQL database, or a Microsoft Fabric warehouse or SQL endpoint — with a SQL login or an Entra service principal.

fields.name: auth
fields.label: Sign in with
fields.help: sql: a SQL login. entra: an Entra (Azure AD) service principal — Azure SQL and Fabric.

fields.name: user
fields.label: User
fields.help: A login that can only read (db_datareader): Superatom checks every query is a read, but SQL Server has no read-only session.

fields.name: encrypt
fields.label: Encrypt
fields.help: true (the default) unless the server has no certificate.

setup.title: Where the server is
setup.say:
The SQL Server's address as the engine reaches it — for Azure SQL or Fabric, the server name ending .database.windows.net (or the Fabric SQL endpoint).

If the server has a firewall (Azure: Networking → firewall rules), let the engine's machine in first.

setup.title: Sign in
setup.say: A SQL login, or an Entra (Azure AD) app that may read. For a SQL login, run this as an admin (choose a password, name your database):

copy.label: Make a read-only login

fix.say: Entra refused the app: check the tenant ID, the client ID and that the secret has not expired — and that the app is a user of the database (CREATE USER [app name] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER).
